newsitem.title: INDIA: India seeks a system to right its awry democracy.
newsitem.headline: India seeks a system to right its awry democracy.

text.p: The fall of two governments within a year has set Indian parties searching for a political system that will guarantee stability without undermining half a century of democracy, political analysts said.

In the 50th year since gaining freedom from British rule, Indians had no clue on Saturday as to which prime minister would traditionally hoist the national flag at Delhi's Moghul Red Fort on August 15, celebrated as Independence Day.
Plans have been put on hold to invite world leaders to the showcase event in August of the world's largest democracy, albeit with an increasingly unstable parliament, officials said.

The latest political crisis was triggered by the fall of Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's 10-month old government on Friday when he was defeated in a vote of confidence with the help of his ally-turned-foe, the Congress party.
Last year, the right-wing Hindu Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) was forced to resign after a mere 12 days in office in a hung parliament following an inconclusive general election.
"This kind of frequent threat to government is not good for India," former lower house speaker Shivraj Patil told parliament during Friday's debate on the confidence vote.
"We should look at some alternative, perhaps the German model," Patil said.
He argued that a German chancellor's job was more secure than the Indian prime minister's five-year tenure because he could not be voted out unless a successor was named.

"I believe we should look at a presidential form of government," the outgoing Finance Minister P. Chidambaram, whose widely-acclaimed budget has been ensnared in the political turmoil, said in a recent television interview.
"I would favour something like the French system, which guarantees political continuity even if the president or parliament gets stuck in a crisis," Chidambaram said.
India adopted the British Westminster-type parliamentary model under a Congress government in 1947, led by then prime minister Jawahar Lal Nehru.
Similar systems in India's neighbouring countries, also former British colonies, have had a chequered life, with Bangladesh and Pakistan falling to spells of military dictatorship.

They subsequently returned to parliamentary systems, even clipping some of the powers of their presidents. Sri Lanka, to India's south, has a presidential government despite its promised reversal to parliamentary rule.
One newspaper said comparison with Pakistan was inescapable.
"At least pass the budget," the Indian Express exhorted parliamentarians, due to discuss Chidambaram's budget on April 21.

"And quickly, find a way of maintaining the foreign policy momentum even if it means learning from Pakistan whose democracy we once held in such superior, self-righteous scorn," the paper said in an editorial.

Ironically, Deve Gowda was celebrated as the leader of the country's largest ever coalition government, its 13 members comprising communists, low-caste Hindu regional groups and free market ideologues.

Faced by the prospect of a mid-term poll if no successor to Deve Gowda is found, deputies urged the badly divided parliament's major parties to bury their differences and form a national government to stave off the looming crisis.
"We plead with the members to consider joining hands in a national government," Surjeet Singh Barnala, a former minister, told parliament.
"Let us redeem ourselves with the people who may otherwise never forgive us for this betrayal," Barnala urged lawmakers moments before Deve Gowda's government lost the trust vote.
